youtube_title: The Floating Home the Supreme Court Said Wasn't a Vessel — Too Late 🦝⚖️
caption: In Lozman v. Riviera Beach (2013), the Supreme Court held a floating home wasn't a 'vessel' because it wasn't designed to a practical degree for carrying people or things over water. The home had already been sold and destroyed.
script: A city took a man's house, declared it a boat, and destroyed it. Then the Supreme Court said it was never a boat. [disclaimer] This is a real Supreme Court case from twenty thirteen. Lozman versus the City of Riviera Beach. Fane Lozman lived in a floating home. Basically a plywood house sitting on an empty box that floats. He got into fights with the city marina. So the city sued him under the law of ships and the sea, for docking fees and trespassing. But to do that, his house had to count as a ship! And the lower courts said, sure, it's a ship. It floats. You can tow it. Done. So his home was ordered sold. The city bought it at auction. And then they destroyed it! Brutal! Then the Supreme Court stepped in. And it said, no. Not everything that floats is a ship. The real test is whether a normal person would look at it and think it's built to carry people or stuff across the water. This house had no steering. No engine. It just looked like a home. So it was not a ship! The case still mattered, because there was money set aside for him if he won. But the win came way too late for the house. And floating homes still have to follow the rules, and his normal debts didn't disappear. [loop] So before you call your houseboat a ship, remember

script_old: A city treated this man's floating home like a ship, and it was sold and destroyed before the Supreme Court said it was never a vessel. This is Lozman versus the City of Riviera Beach, from twenty thirteen. Fane Lozman lived in a floating home: a plywood, house-shaped structure, kept afloat by an empty space underneath. After disputes with the city's marina, the city sued in admiralty, the federal law of ships and the sea, seeking dockage fees and trespass damages. For that, the house had to count as a vessel. The lower courts said it did. It floats, and it can be towed. The home was ordered sold, and the city bought it at auction and had it destroyed. Then the Supreme Court ruled, seven to two. Not every floating structure is a vessel. The test is whether a reasonable observer would consider it designed, to a practical degree, for carrying people or things over water. This house had no steering, no engine, and looked like ordinary living quarters. So, not a vessel. The case wasn't moot, because a bond secured his possible recovery. But the ruling came too late for the house. And it doesn't exempt floating homes from regulation, or erase ordinary debts. [loop] So before you call your houseboat a ship, remember
